chapters.title: Chapter 5: Matching the Method to the Business

lessons.title: Valuing Stable Compounders: FMCG and IT Services

children.text: Some Indian companies seem almost boring: they sell soap, biscuits, paint or software services, they grow year after year, they rarely need to borrow, and they return cash to shareholders. They also trade at some of the highest multiples on NSE and BSE, often 40 to 60 times earnings or more. Is the market irrational, or does something about these businesses justify such prices? This chapter matches valuation methods to business types, and it starts with the companies where the DCF works best.

body.text: For stable compounders, the valuation question is not whether they will grow, but for how long they can keep earning far above their cost of capital. Their value sits in that long tail, so lead with a DCF that has a long explicit period and a realistic fade.

children.text: combines three traits from Chapter 1: high return on capital, low reinvestment needs and predictable demand. Indian FMCG and large IT services companies are the classic examples, but their economics differ in important ways.

markDefs.definition: A business that can reinvest part of its profits at high returns on capital for many years, growing earnings steadily while still generating substantial free cash flow.

body.title: FMCG vs IT services: economics that drive value

columns.label: FMCG
points: Revenue: volume × price and mix, across urban and rural India
Key costs: raw materials such as palm oil, wheat, crude derivatives; advertising
Capital needs: low; distributors often pay faster than suppliers are paid, so working capital can be negative
Moat: brands, distribution reach into lakhs of retail outlets, pricing power
Main risks: input cost spikes, rural demand slowdowns, competition from new-age and regional brands

columns.label: IT services
points: Revenue: mostly in US dollars and euros; driven by deal wins, client spending and headcount
Key costs: employee salaries, mostly in rupees; subcontractors; travel and visas
Capital needs: very low; mainly offices and laptops
Moat: long client relationships, delivery scale, domain expertise
Main risks: client spending cuts, wage inflation, attrition, rupee appreciation, technology shifts

body.text: Negative working capital is a hidden advantage. When an FMCG company collects cash from distributors before paying its suppliers, growth releases cash instead of consuming it. In a DCF, the working capital part of reinvestment can be negative, which lifts free cash flow above net profit.

children.text: Annapurna Consumer Products Ltd is a fictional debt-free NSE-listed FMCG company selling packaged foods and home care products. Revenue is ₹10,000 crore with a 20.0% EBIT margin. It needs only ₹1 of capital for every ₹4 of additional sales, holds ₹1,000 crore of cash and has 100 crore shares. With a beta of 0.6, a 6.5% risk-free rate and a 7.0% ERP, its cost of equity, and WACC, is 10.7%. The shares trade at ₹780, about 50 times earnings.

The structure of the DCF matters more than any single input. A standard five-year model with growth fading quickly and returns on new capital falling to WACC will badly undervalue a business like this. Watch what happens as the assumptions reflect a longer-lasting moat.

body.caption: Annapurna Consumer Products: DCF value under four structures (illustrative)

cells: 5 years at 12%, fade to 5%; terminal RONIC = WACC
5 years at 12%, fade to 5%; terminal RONIC 20%
10 years at 12%, fade to 5%; terminal RONIC 30%
15 years at 12%, fade to 5%; terminal RONIC 30%

body.title: Annapurna: DCF value per share by structure vs ₹780 market price

children.text: Variant A, a textbook model where excess returns disappear after the forecast, values Annapurna at ₹277, about 17.8 times earnings. Allowing the moat to persist in the terminal value (B) lifts it to ₹332. Stretching high growth to 10 and then 15 years, with returns on new capital near 30% (C and D), raises it to ₹438 and ₹528, still well below the ₹780 market price. Solving directly, at a 10.7% cost of equity and a 30% terminal RONIC, ₹780 requires about 28 years of 12% growth before the fade begins.

Now change one more input. Investors often accept a lower return from steady, low-risk consumer businesses than CAPM suggests. At a 9.5% cost of equity, the same price requires about 18 years of 12% growth. For stable compounders, the discount rate and the duration of growth together explain most of the gap between a textbook DCF and the market price, which is why both deserve far more attention than next year's earnings.

body.label: What the market price is really saying
body.value: About 28 years of 12% growth, then a long, profitable fade
body.context: At a 10.7% cost of equity, that is an exceptionally long run of high growth, which very few companies anywhere sustain. Even at a lower 9.5% cost of equity, about 18 years are needed. Buying at this price means betting that the brands, distribution and returns stay dominant for decades, with little room for error if growth slows early or a competitor erodes returns.

body.text: Two opposite mistakes are common. Setting terminal RONIC equal to WACC for a company with a durable brand ignores the moat and undervalues it. Setting RONIC at 40% and growth at 8% forever assumes the moat never weakens and overvalues it. Choose a terminal RONIC that reflects how durable you genuinely believe the advantage is, and test both ends.

body.caption: Key drivers for Indian FMCG valuations

cells: Growth driven mainly by price increases is less durable than volume-led growth
Quarterly results commentary on underlying volume growth
Margins at a peak when commodity prices are low will normalise
Gross margin trend; commentary on palm oil, crude and agri inputs
Rural slowdowns hit mass-market brands hardest
Management commentary, monsoon and rural wage data
Cutting ad spend flatters margins today at the expense of brand strength
Advertising and promotion as % of sales
Direct reach into outlets supports growth and pricing power
Quick commerce, D2C brands and regional players can erode share
Channel mix disclosures, market share data

children.text: What Drives Value in IT Services

Tungabhadra Technologies Ltd is a fictional mid-sized Indian IT services company. It earns nearly all its revenue in US dollars, has a 21.0% EBIT margin, and employee costs equal to 55.0% of revenue. About 70% of its total costs are incurred in rupees.

body.title: Tungabhadra Technologies: where each ₹100 of revenue goes (illustrative)

body.caption: How the rupee and wages move Tungabhadra's EBIT margin, before any hedging or pricing offsets

cells: Salaries rise 1% with no price increase
Annual salary hike of 7% with no offsets

children.text: In practice, companies offset wage hikes with price increases, better utilisation, a younger employee pyramid and automation, and they hedge part of their currency exposure, so actual margin moves are smaller. But the table shows why two variables outside management's control, the rupee and wage inflation, belong in every IT services forecast and scenario.

body.caption: Key drivers for Indian IT services valuations

cells: Total contract value of new deals signals future revenue
Revenue growth excluding currency effects shows real demand
Heavy exposure to one client or sector, such as banking or retail, raises risk
Revenue by top clients and verticals
High attrition raises hiring and training costs
Dividends and buybacks return most free cash flow; acquisitions add risk

body.text: Large Indian IT services companies typically return a large share of their free cash flow through dividends and buybacks, and hold significant cash. Value the operating business with a DCF, add surplus cash separately, and remember from Chapter 4 that a cash-adjusted P/E for a highly rated company is usually higher than the headline figure.

cells: DCF with a 10 to 15 year explicit period and a slow fade
DCF with a 10 year explicit period; scenario-based on demand cycles
Very low; mainly capex on offices and technology
Well above WACC if brands are durable
Above WACC, but test for technology disruption
Reverse DCF on implied growth duration; P/E vs true peers
P/E and cash-adjusted P/E vs peers of similar size and growth

body.title: The wage hike
body.prompt: An IT services company's employee costs equal 55% of revenue. If it gives a 5% salary increase with no price increases, utilisation gains or currency benefit, by how many percentage points does its EBIT margin fall?
body.explanation: Employee costs rise by 55% × 5% = 2.75% of revenue, so EBIT margin falls by 2.75 percentage points. That is why companies work hard to offset wage hikes with pricing, utilisation and a younger employee mix.

body.title: Growth that releases cash
body.prompt: An FMCG company's net working capital is negative, at -10% of revenue. If its revenue grows by ₹1,000 crore next year and the ratio holds, how much cash does the change in working capital release, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Net working capital moves from -10% of the old revenue to -10% of the new revenue, a change of -10% × ₹1,000 crore = -₹100 crore. A more negative working capital balance means ₹100 crore of cash is released, adding to free cash flow.

body.title: Choosing terminal RONIC
body.question: You are valuing a market-leading Indian FMCG company with dominant brands, national distribution and a 60-year history of high returns. Which terminal assumption is most defensible?
options: RONIC equal to WACC, because all excess returns disappear in the long run
RONIC meaningfully above WACC, tested with a downside case closer to WACC
RONIC of 80%, matching its current ROCE, forever
Terminal growth of 12%, matching its recent revenue growth
body.explanation: Durable brands and distribution can sustain returns above the cost of capital for a very long time, so RONIC equal to WACC is too harsh. But assuming today's extraordinary ROCE forever, or growth far above nominal GDP forever, is too generous. Use a well-reasoned level above WACC and test the downside.

body.title: Distributor cash
body.textWithBlank: An FMCG company that collects cash from distributors before it pays its suppliers operates with ___ working capital.
body.explanation: Negative working capital means growth releases cash rather than consuming it, one reason FMCG free cash flow can exceed net profit.

body.title: The price-led FMCG rally
body.scenario: Tanvi, a Bhopal-based investor, is looking at a listed FMCG company trading at 58× earnings. Last year it reported 11% revenue growth and a record 22% EBIT margin. Reading the results, she finds: underlying volume growth was only 2%, with the rest from price increases; gross margin expanded because palm oil prices fell sharply; advertising spend was cut from 11% to 8% of sales; and rural demand, which is 40% of its sales, has been weak for three quarters. A broker's DCF extrapolates 11% growth and a 22% margin for ten years.
body.prompt: What is wrong with the broker's DCF, and how should Tanvi model this company?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Growth quality. With volume growth of 2%, most of the 11% came from price increases. Price-led growth is less durable, especially when input costs are falling, because competitors and retailers push for price cuts. The base case should forecast volume and price separately, with price growth closer to inflation.
2. Peak margins. The 22% margin benefits from unusually low palm oil prices and a cut in advertising. Both are likely to reverse. The base case margin should be closer to the multi-year average, with advertising restored to protect the brands.
3. Rural weakness. With 40% of sales from rural India and three weak quarters, near-term volume growth should reflect that, with recovery as a scenario rather than an assumption.
4. Ten years of 11% at 22% margins is not a base case. It combines a peak margin with price-led growth for a decade.

How to model it: forecast revenue as volume plus price and mix; normalise gross margin for input costs and restore advertising; use a long explicit period with a gradual fade, since this is a genuine compounder; set terminal RONIC above WACC but test a lower case; then run a reverse DCF to see what 58× implies about growth duration. Only if that looks achievable on normalised margins and realistic volume growth is the price justified.

points: Stable compounders combine high returns on capital, low reinvestment and predictable demand. DCF works best for them.
Their value lies in how long excess returns last, so use a long explicit period, a slow fade and a terminal RONIC above WACC where the moat is durable.
A short model with returns falling to WACC will undervalue a genuine compounder; a model with peak margins and high growth forever will overvalue it.
For FMCG, separate volume from price growth, normalise input-cost-driven margins, and watch advertising and rural demand.
For IT services, model constant currency growth, the rupee and wage inflation explicitly, and value surplus cash separately.
Use a reverse DCF to translate a high multiple into implied growth duration, and judge whether that is achievable.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Annapurna Consumer Products Ltd, Tungabhadra Technologies Ltd, the other companies described and the individuals named are fictional, and all figures are illustrative.
